title: Trump's crusade against voting by mail: what you need to know

image.caption: A drop box for mail-in voting is pictured in San Francisco. Some 47 million people voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election, won by Donald Trump. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

blocks.text: World·CBC Explains

For months, U.S. President Donald Trump has tried to impose new restrictions on voting by mail, a method used by roughly one-third of American voters. The U.S. Supreme Court has put an end to Trump's plan.
Roughly one-third of U.S. voters cast ballots by mail, typically more Democrats than Republicans
For months, U.S. President Donald Trump has tried to impose new restrictions on voting by mail, a method used at election time by nearly one-third of American voters.

And yet, with the crucial midterms less than seven weeks away, the U.S. Supreme Court has halted a Trump administration plan that could have denied millions the chance to cast mail-in ballots. Here's what you need to know.
How important is mail-in voting in the U.S.?
Tens of millions of Americans use mail-in ballots to vote in both presidential and midterm elections.
The proportion of Americans voting by mail increased gradually through the 2010s to reach 25 per cent in 2018, then spiked to 43 per cent in 2020 with the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic.
About 30 per cent of the 158 million votes cast in the 2024 presidential election were mail-in ballots, according to the official report by the U.S. Election Assistance Commission.
These figures are all far higher than the proportion voting by mail in federal elections in Canada.

Although a report by Elections Canada shows a record 1.25 million people voted by mail in the 2025 general election using the special ballot process, that represents just 6.3 per cent of the nearly 20 million total ballots cast across the country.
The truth behind Trump’s push to ban mail-in voting | About That
What are Trump's problems with voting by mail?

Trump raged against states that expanded access to mail-in voting for the 2020 presidential election, then claimed without evidence that the election was stolen from him because of fraud, with mail-in voting at the centre of his complaints.

Fraud in voting by mail is exceedingly rare, found in about four cases out of every 10 million mail-in ballots cast, according to research by the Brookings Institution, a non-partisan think-tank in Washington.

Since his return to the White House last year, Trump's complaints have largely focused on unsubstantiated claims that mail-in ballots make it easier for large numbers of non-citizens to vote illegally and help the Democrats win.
Who votes by mail?

Although millions of registered Republicans — including Trump — have opted to vote by mail in past elections, there's evidence that restricting mail-in ballots could give an advantage to the Republicans in tight congressional races and swing states.

Research by the MIT Election Data Lab and the Pew Research Center suggests that registered Democrats were more likely than registered Republicans to vote by mail in 2020 and 2024, although the gap narrowed in the most recent presidential election.
The research also indicates that Americans 65 and older are the age group most likely to choose mail-in voting.
How did Trump try to restrict mail-in ballots?
Trump's plan was designed to give the U.S. Postal Service — a federal agency controlled by the administration — authority over voters' eligibility to receive mail-in ballots.
This would be a departure from the U.S. voting system, in which states hold the legal power to manage and conduct elections.
In March, Trump issued an executive order directing the Department of Homeland Security to and the Social Security Administration to create lists of U.S. citizens eligible to vote.
In turn, Trump's order directed the postal service to send ballots only to people on the lists and to develop a system for tracking who voted by mail.
'Literally crazy': Critics slam Trump over election interference claims

The plan would have also forced states to redesign their ballot packages to meet new postal service rules, which many states said would be impossible to do in time for the election, potentially disenfranchising everyone who wanted to vote by mail.

Led by California, states launched a legal challenge and a federal court judge slapped a series of injunctions on the plan. On Monday in an emergency ruling, the Supreme Court denied the administration's request to lift the injunction.
What did Trump say about the ruling?

In a lengthy post on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday, Trump decried what he called the "totally CORRUPT and out of control Mail-In voting 'disaster,' which is a laughing stock all over the World."
He called the court's ruling horrible and said it "makes cheating ... a much easier thing to do."
He also blasted the court for rendering "some of the most destructive, hurtful, and damaging decisions in our Country’s history."
All three of the justices who Trump appointed to the court in his first term denied the administration's application in the case.
What happens next?
While it appears that the Supreme Court ruling paves the way for mail-in voting for November's midterm elections to take place as normal, this is likely not the last you'll hear from Trump about it.
If the Republicans lose control of the House or the Senate in the midterms, voters' rights groups have raised concerns that Trump will try to cast doubt on the accuracy of the results.

items: Your guide to the U.S. midterms, and why they're crucial for Donald Trump
U.S. Supreme Court rejects Trump's bid to restrict mail-in ballots ahead of November midterms

blocks.text: Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters Tuesday that the administration's efforts to curtail mail-in voting are about ensuring the integrity of the vote.

Trump's "efforts to make sure that we have free and fair elections are not going to stop in November or thereafter," said Blanche, who acted as the president's defence lawyer in the criminal case alleging he attempted to interfere with the 2020 presidential election.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Mike Crawley is a correspondent for CBC News, based in Washington. He began his career as a newspaper reporter in B.C., spent six years as a freelance journalist in various parts of Africa, then joined the CBC in 2005. Mike reported on Ontario politics for 15 years. He was born and raised in Saint John, N.B.
